text: There is no doubt that life is given us, not to be enjoyed, but to be overcome--to be got over.
plain: Life is something you get through, not something you collect pleasures from.

text: It is prudent and wise, I say, to reduce one's claims, if only for the reason that it is extremely easy to be very unhappy; while to be very happy is not indeed difficult, but quite impossible.
plain: Expect less and you get hurt less. Constant bliss was never on the menu.

text: To desire to get rid of an evil is a definite object, but to desire a better fortune than one has is blind folly.
plain: Fix a real problem. Chasing a vague better life just keeps you restless.

text: Joy is like the gold in the Australian mines--found only now and then, as it were, by the caprice of chance, and according to no rule or law; oftenest in very little grains, and very seldom in heaps.
plain: Joy shows up in small grains at random moments, not on schedule at the big events.

text: Everything in the world is like a hollow nut; there is little kernel anywhere, and when it does exist, it is still more rare to find it in the shell.
plain: Most shiny things are empty inside. The real stuff is rare and hides.

text: To be irritated by trifles, a man must be well off; for in misfortunes trifles are unfelt.
plain: If small stuff bugs you, your life is going fine. Real trouble makes trifles disappear.

text: To make extensive preparations for life--no matter what form they may take--is one of the greatest and commonest of follies.
plain: Stop preparing to live. Start doing the thing now.

text: Instead of finding, as we expected, pleasure, happiness, joy, we get experience, insight, knowledge--a real and permanent blessing, instead of a fleeting and illusory one.
plain: You chase happiness and end up with wisdom, which lasts longer.

text: In their search for gold, the alchemists discovered other things--gunpowder, china, medicines, the laws of nature. There is a sense in which we are all alchemists.
plain: The goal you chase may fail, but what you find on the way can be worth more.

text: Distance, which makes objects look small to the outward eye, makes them look big to the eye of thought. The present alone is true and actual; it is the only time which possesses full reality, and our existence lies in it exclusively.
plain: Past and future loom bigger in your head than they are. Only now is real.

text: It is the height of folly to refuse the present hour of happiness, or wantonly to spoil it by vexation at by-gones or uneasiness about what is to come.
plain: Don't ruin a good hour by stewing over the past or the future.

text: We should always collect that To-day comes only once, and never returns. We fancy that it will come again to-morrow; but To-morrow is another day, which, in its turn, comes once only.
plain: Today does not repeat. Tomorrow is a different day, not a refund.

text: A thousand gay and pleasant hours are wasted in ill-humor; we let them slip by unenjoyed, and sigh for them in vain when the sky is overcast.
plain: You will miss these good hours later. Notice them now.

text: Limitations always make for happiness.
plain: Fewer options, fewer worries. Narrow focus is peaceful.

text: Experience of the world may be looked upon as a kind of text, to which reflection and knowledge form the commentary.
plain: Living teaches nothing unless you stop and think about it.

text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone; and if he does not love solitude, he will not love freedom; for it is only when he is alone that he is really free.
plain: You only get to be yourself when no one is watching. Learn to like your own company.

text: The more a man has in himself, the less others can be to him.
plain: The richer your inner life, the less you need the crowd.

text: Ordinary people are sociable and complaisant just from the very opposite feeling;--to bear others' company is easier for them than to bear their own.
plain: Many people are around others because they can't stand being alone with themselves.

text: It is the monotony of his own nature that makes a man find solitude intolerable.
plain: If being alone feels unbearable, it's because there's not much going on inside yet.

text: Peace of mind is impossible without a considerable amount of solitude.
plain: You need hours alone to be calm. No way around it.

text: To be soon on friendly, or even affectionate, terms with solitude is like winning a gold mine; but this is not something which everybody can do.
plain: Being comfortable alone is a rare, valuable skill.

text: To be alone is the fate of all great minds--a fate deplored at times, but still always chosen as the less grievous of two evils.
plain: Anyone doing something great ends up alone sometimes. It's the cheaper cost.

text: The young should early be trained to bear being left alone; for it is a source of happiness and peace of mind.
plain: Learn to be alone while you're young. It pays off for life.

text: Society is in this respect like a fire--the wise man warming himself at a proper distance from it; not coming too close, like the fool, who, on getting scorched, runs away and shivers in solitude, loud in his complaint that the fire burns.
plain: Enjoy people from a safe distance. Don't get burned and then blame the fire.

text: Envy is natural to man; and still, it is at once a vice and a source of misery.
plain: Envy feels normal and it only hurts you.

text: See well to your girths, and then ride on boldly.
plain: Prepare properly, then commit and stop second guessing.

text: If we have made obvious mistakes, we should not try, as we generally do, to gloss them over, or to find something to excuse or extenuate them; we should admit to ourselves that we have committed faults, and open our eyes wide to all their enormity, in order that we may firmly resolve to avoid them in time to come.
plain: Own your mistakes fully, no excuses, so you don't repeat them.

text: We should give no play to imagination here; for imagination is not judgment--it only conjures up visions, inducing an unprofitable and often very painful mood.
plain: Your imagination invents scary stories. That's not the same as thinking.

text: Night gives a black look to everything, whatever it may be.
plain: Everything looks worse at night. Wait for morning before you judge.

text: Do not shorten the morning by getting up late, or waste it in unworthy occupations or in talk; look upon it as the quintessence of life, as to a certain extent sacred.
plain: Protect your mornings. They're your best hours.

text: Each day is a little life: every waking and rising a little birth, every fresh morning a little youth, every going to rest and sleep a little death.
plain: Every day is a full small life. Treat it that way.

text: The smallest annoyance, whether it comes from our fellow-men or from the things around us, may swell up into a monster of dreadful aspect, putting us at our wits' end--and all because we go on brooding over our troubles and painting them in the most glaring colors and on the largest scale.
plain: Brooding blows small irritations up into monsters.

text: It is much better to take a very calm and prosaic view of what is disagreeable; for that is the easiest way of bearing it.
plain: Look at the bad thing flatly, without drama. It hurts less.

text: If you hold small objects close to your eyes, you limit your field of vision and shut out the world.
plain: Small problems held too close block out everything else.

text: It is a source of consolation to look back upon those great misfortunes which never happened.
plain: Most of the disasters you feared never came. Remember that.

text: Our thoughts must be arranged, as it were, in little drawers, so that we may open one without disturbing any of the others.
plain: Handle one problem at a time. Close the others.

text: Nothing will protect us from external compulsion so much as the control of ourselves; and, as Seneca says, to submit yourself to reason is the way to make everything else submit to you--si tibi vis omnia subjicere, te subjice rationi.
plain: Rule yourself or the world will rule you.

text: Effort, struggles with difficulties! that is as natural to a man as grubbing in the ground is to a mole.
plain: Struggle is your natural habitat, not a defect.

text: Let everyone, then, do something, according to the measure of his capacities. To have no regular work, no set sphere of activity--what a miserable thing it is!
plain: Having no work to do is misery. Get something to build.

text: To overcome difficulties is to experience the full delight of existence, no matter where the obstacles are encountered; whether in the affairs of life, in commerce or business; or in mental effort--the spirit of inquiry that tries to master its subject.
plain: The joy of life is in beating obstacles.

text: There is always something pleasurable in the struggle and the victory.
plain: The fight itself and the win are both satisfying.

text: There is a direct pleasure in seeing work grow under one's hands day by day, until at last it is finished.
plain: Watching something you build grow daily is its own reward.

text: A man should avoid being led on by the phantoms of his imagination.
plain: Don't steer your life by daydreams of how it will feel.

text: The way to harden the body is to impose a great deal of labor and effort upon it in the days of good health,--to exercise it, both as a whole and in its several parts, and to habituate it to withstand all kinds of noxious influences.
plain: Train hard while healthy so the body can take hits later.

text: It is most important to allow the brain the full measure of sleep which is required to restore it; for sleep is to a man's whole nature what winding up is to a clock.
plain: Sleep is what winds you back up. Don't skimp.

text: The brain can be ruined by overstrain, just like the eyes.
plain: Overworking your mind breaks it like any other muscle.

text: In making his way through life, a man will find it useful to be ready and able to do two things: to look ahead and to overlook: the one will protect him from loss and injury, the other from disputes and squabbles.
plain: Plan ahead, and let petty stuff slide.

text: To become indignant at their conduct is as foolish as to be angry with a stone because it rolls into your path.
plain: People act per their nature. Raging at them is like raging at a rock.

text: Great minds are like eagles, and build their nest in some lofty solitude.
plain: Great people live apart from the crowd.

text: No man can see over his own height.
plain: You can only recognize in others what you already have in you.

text: Intellect is invisible to the man who has none.
plain: Some people can't see your quality. Don't take it personally.

text: Men are like children, in that, if you spoil them, they become naughty.
plain: Too much indulgence makes people entitled.

text: The only way to attain superiority in dealing with men, is to let it be seen that you are independent of them.
plain: Needing nobody gives you the upper hand.

text: A man shows his character just in the way in which he deals with trifles,--for then he is off his guard.
plain: Watch how someone handles small things. That's who they are.

text: There is nothing, absolutely nothing, that a man cannot forget,--but not himself, his own character.
plain: You can forget anything except who you are.

text: In savage countries they eat one another, in civilized they deceive one another; and that is what people call the way of the world!
plain: We swapped violence for lying and called it civilization.

text: To affect a quality, and to plume yourself upon it, is just to confess that you have not got it.
plain: Bragging about a trait shows you lack it.

text: He who criticises others, works at the reformation of himself.
plain: Judging others sharpens your own standards.

text: We require a looking-glass for the due dressing of our morals.
plain: Other people's flaws show you your own.

text: Your friends will tell you that they are sincere; your enemies are really so.
plain: Friends flatter you. Enemies tell you the truth.

text: A friend in need, as the saying goes, is rare. Nay, it is just the contrary; no sooner have you made a friend than he is in need, and asks for a loan.
plain: Everyone's a friend until they need something.

text: A man must be still a greenhorn in the ways of the world, if he imagines that he can make himself popular in society by exhibiting intelligence and discernment.
plain: Showing off how smart you are does not make people like you.

text: To show your intelligence and discernment is only an indirect way of reproaching other people for being dull and incapable.
plain: Flexing your brains makes others feel stupid, so they resent you.

text: To combine politeness with pride is a masterpiece of wisdom.
plain: Be courteous and still keep your self-respect.

text: Never combat any man's opinion; for though you reached the age of Methuselah, you would never have done setting him right upon all the absurd things that he believes.
plain: You can't correct everyone. Save your energy.

text: If you want your judgment to be accepted, express it coolly and without passion.
plain: Say it calmly if you want to be believed.

text: Even when you are fully justified in praising yourself, you should never be seduced into doing so.
plain: Let your work speak. Self-praise backfires.

text: Prudence exacts that a wide gulf should be fixed between what we think and what we say.
plain: Keep a gap between your thoughts and your mouth.

text: Do not tell a friend anything that you would conceal from an enemy.
plain: Keep real secrets to yourself.

text: A secret is in my custody, if I keep it; but should it escape me, it is I who am the prisoner.
plain: Once a secret leaves your mouth, it owns you.

text: The tree of silence bears the fruit of peace.
plain: Staying quiet keeps you calm.

text: Money is never spent to so much advantage as when you have been cheated out of it; for at one stroke you have purchased prudence.
plain: Getting scammed is tuition. At least learn something.

text: Give way neither to love nor to hate, is one-half of worldly wisdom: say nothing and believe nothing, the other half.
plain: Don't be ruled by love or hate, and don't take people at their word.

text: Anger and hatred should never be shown otherwise than in what you do; and feelings will be all the more effective in action, in so far as you avoid the exhibition of them in any other way. It is only cold-blooded animals whose bite is poisonous.
plain: Don't shout your anger. Channel it into action.

text: Most men are so thoroughly subjective that nothing really interests them but themselves.
plain: People are mostly thinking about themselves, not you.

text: He who can see truly in the midst of general infatuation is like a man whose watch keeps good time, when all clocks in the town in which he lives are wrong.
plain: Being right when everyone's wrong is lonely. Keep your time anyway.
